phonemes.desc: Palato-alveolar affricate [tʃ], as in English 'chin'. The initial cluster is a common Murrinh-Patha orthographic convention for a single consonant sound.
Short vowels [i] and [ɪ] alternating in an unstressed syllable sequence; Murrinh-Patha is stress-timed, with vowel quality governed by syllable position.
Final [m] and [n] are plain bilabial and alveolar nasals; the name ends in a closed syllable common in Murrinh-Patha proper names.

pronunciation.approximation: 'CHIN-ih-min' — stress the first syllable, keep the vowels short and clear, and pronounce the initial 'tj' as English 'ch'.

kin.label: Murrinh-Patha
kin.form: Tjinimin — the ancestral being who appears in Murrinh-Patha Dreaming narratives collected by W. E. H. Stanner.

kin.label: English gloss
kin.form: No transparent English etymology; the name is treated as a proper noun for an ancestral figure.

pronunciation.note: The PuniCodex lexicon classifies Tjinimin as 'Trickster, Moth Man', but the published Murrinh-Patha sources associate the figure with the bat (flying fox) and the Rainbow Serpent Kunmanggur. The 'moth' label is not attested in the scholarly record and should be treated as provisional. Because the name is already written in basic Latin letters, the Unicode restoration capitalizes the initial letter only; no diacritic or original-script mark is recovered. The entry is therefore Tier 2.

domains.title: Ancestor of the Peoples
domains.subtitle: Bat, Rainbow Serpent, and Ancestral Law
domains.lead: Tjinimin is an ancestral being in the mythology of the Murrinh-Patha peoples of the Daly River region, Northern Territory. He is remembered as an ancestor of the Australian peoples, closely associated with the bat or flying fox and with Kunmanggur, the great Rainbow Serpent. His story turns on a quarrel, a vow, and the origin of the bat's short nose — a narrative that encodes law, social restraint, and the place of humans within the Dreaming.

cards.name: Ancestry
cards.desc: Tjinimin is identified in Murrinh-Patha tradition as an ancestor of the Australian peoples, a foundational figure in the genealogical memory of the Daly River communities.

cards.name: Bat and Flying Fox
cards.desc: The figure is associated with the bat; a key myth explains the bat's short nose as the result of Tjinimin's vow and transformation.

cards.name: Rainbow Serpent
cards.desc: Tjinimin's narrative is bound to Kunmanggur, the Rainbow Serpent, whose consorts and authority set the moral stakes of the story.

cards.name: Trickster and Law
cards.desc: His attempt to transgress social boundaries, his defeat, and his lasting vow form a cautionary tale about desire, consequence, and the establishment of ancestral law.

symbols.name: Bat or flying fox
symbols.meaning: The animal form and kinship emblem linked to Tjinimin; the myth of the short nose explains the bat's distinctive face.

symbols.name: Rainbow Serpent (Kunmanggur)
symbols.meaning: The great water-spirit and law-giver whose authority Tjinimin challenges; the serpent marks the boundary between acceptable and forbidden desire.

symbols.name: The upside-down tree
symbols.meaning: The place where Tjinimin hung after his defeat, looking at the stars and making his vow of abstinence.

symbols.name: Stars
symbols.meaning: The night sky that Tjinimin contemplated while suspended; a symbol of reflection, withdrawal, and transformation.

mythology.lead: The principal Murrinh-Patha narrative of Tjinimin, recorded by W. E. H. Stanner from the Daly River country, is a compact myth of boundary-crossing and transformation. It explains kinship, animal form, and the moral order through a single ancestral episode — and its fuller ritual meanings remain with the custodians who still keep it.

myths.title: The Quarrel with Kunmanggur
myths.text: In the beginning-time, when the ancestral beings walked in their first forms, Tjinimin set his desire against Kunmanggur, the great Rainbow Serpent, the water-being whose body made the rivers and whose authority ordered the relations between all the ancestral peoples. He coveted Kunmanggur's consorts, the Green Parrot-Girls, and pressed his claim in the quarrel that the old men still tell. Stanner recorded the narrative in the mid-twentieth century from Murrinh-Patha speakers at Port Keats (Wadeye), and it must be said that the published account is the publicly speakable layer of the story: senior custodians hold fuller versions that ethnography does not print. What the published telling makes plain is the myth's charge — desire aimed at what is not one's own, aimed, moreover, at the possessions of the most powerful law-giver in the country. The quarrel defines the boundary of the permissible by showing what it costs to cross it.

myths.title: The Vow beneath the Stars
myths.text: Defeated in the quarrel, Tjinimin withdrew from the world in the most literal way the country allows: he hung himself upside down in a tree, head toward the earth, feet toward the sky, and there he gazed at the stars. In that suspension, between the ground of the living and the camp of the dead, he made a vow that the Murrinh-Patha tell as absolute: he would never lie with a woman again. No council imposed this sentence and no serpent demanded it — the old men emphasize that Tjinimin pronounced it himself, and that such a vow, once spoken beneath the stars, binds the speaker past recall. He hung there through the nights, looking down at the world he had forfeited and up at the order he could no longer join. The myth makes law interesting: its deepest form is not punishment from above but sentence passed on oneself, self-exile from the ordinary human sentence of desire and consequence.

myths.title: The Short Nose of the Bat
myths.text: Soon after the vow, the story says, Tjinimin's nose fell off. The detail is the myth's signature: it is the reason, the old men explain, that the bats of the Daly country have short noses — the ancestral being's bodily transformation became the permanent anatomy of the animal with which he is thereafter identified. In Murrinh-Patha understanding this is not merely an etiological curiosity. The bat, the flying fox that camps in the river trees, is kin: its face is the visible record of an ancestral choice, read every evening as the colonies rise at dusk. Tjinimin's punishment and his animal form are the same event — to be changed into the bat is both the consequence of the transgression and its memorial. The myth means that ancestral law is not written anywhere but on the bodies of the country: in the short nose of the bat, in the course of the river, any child can read what happens to those who reach for what the law withholds.

myths.title: The Keeping of the Story
myths.text: The final episode of the Tjinimin narrative is its modern history. W. E. H. Stanner, the Australian anthropologist, worked among the Murrinh-Patha of the Daly River from the 1930s and set down the Tjinimin cycle in his studies of Aboriginal religion (published in the 1950s–60s), moved by what he famously called the 'metaphysical pity' of a tradition that endures against enormous pressure. The story continues to be kept the older way as well: senior men teach it in initiation, holding the restricted meanings close, and recordings sit with AIATSIS in Canberra as the people's own archive. The sources are therefore honest about their limits — what is printed is what may be printed — and the myth's custodians, not its ethnographers, remain its authors. This afterlife completes the story's meaning: a tale about the cost of taking what is not yours is itself handled under a law of custodianship, passed hand to hand, never simply taken.

lore.syncretism: Tjinimin belongs specifically to Murrinh-Patha tradition rather than to the wider cross-cultural networks of the Kimberley Wandjina or Arnhem Land Rainbow Serpent complexes. Within Murrinh-Patha cosmology he is grouped with the ancestor-figures whose stories encode law, kinship, and the origins of animal species. Comparative scholarship sometimes links him to the broader Australian theme of the Moon-Man or to nocturnal transformation myths, but these connections remain speculative; the primary attested context is the Daly River region, and responsible scholarship says no more than the record allows.
lore.culturalLegacy: Tjinimin survives in Murrinh-Patha oral tradition, initiation teaching, and the ethnographic record compiled by W. E. H. Stanner and later scholars. The story is used in initiation contexts to instruct young men in ancestral law, social restraint, and the consequences of transgression, and the bat of the Daly country remains its daily reminder. Unlike the widely commercialised Wandjina imagery of the Kimberley, Murrinh-Patha sacred narratives such as that of Tjinimin are generally restricted to initiated custodians and are not reproduced as open visual art — a form of protection that has kept the story intact but also largely invisible to the wider world. For Murrinh-Patha communities themselves, Tjinimin is family: an ancestor whose face rises with the flying foxes every dusk.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Tjinimin is a difficult ancestor because his story turns on failure rather than triumph. He desires what is not his, loses, withdraws, and is transformed. The myth does not celebrate his ambition; it records the cost of transgression and the permanent mark it leaves on the body. In this he is close to the trickster type, but he is also a cautionary figure: the ancestor whose own choice limits him.

For contemporary readers, Tjinimin raises questions about the relationship between desire and law. What does it mean to make a vow that cannot be undone? How does a community remember the one who overreached and was changed? The bat's short nose is not merely an etiological detail; it is a material reminder that ancestral actions continue to shape the living world.
lore.originalScriptNote: No indigenous writing system is securely attested for Murrinh-Patha proper names in the pre-contact period. The name Tjinimin appears in scholarly transcription using the Latin alphabet, with tj representing a palato-alveolar affricate. The PuniCodex restoration capitalises the initial letter; the ASCII form tjinimin is otherwise identical. Because no diacritic, stress mark, or original-script character is recoverable, the name is classified as Tier 2.

etymology.derivation: The name is a Murrinh-Patha proper noun; its internal etymology is not transparent in the published scholarly record. It is preserved as the name of an ancestral being associated with the bat and the Rainbow Serpent Kunmanggur.

nameVariations.note: Standard scholarly transcription used by W. E. H. Stanner and later sources.

lore.archaeology: No fixed archaeological site is publicly identified with Tjinimin. Murrinh-Patha sacred geography is held by custodians and is not published in open scholarly form. The primary 'site' of the narrative is the Daly River country of the Northern Territory, where the story is maintained through initiation, ceremony, and oral transmission; Stanner's field records and the AIATSIS sound archive are the documentary witnesses.
